newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lafontaine wants EMU on time, with Italy, Spain.
newsitem.headline: Lafontaine wants EMU on time, with Italy, Spain.

text.p: German opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine on Thursday called for European economic and monetary union (EMU) to start on time in 1999, preferably with Italy and Spain included.
Social Democrat (SPD) chief Lafontaine, in an interview with Die Woche weekly, also urged European Union leaders to make getting the region's 18 million unemployed back to work a top priority.
"The fundamentally new approach must be to put employment policy at centre stage in Europe. Economic and monetary union must serve this cause," Lafontaine told Die Woche.
He backed the call by France's new left-wing government to include an employment chapter in the so-called Maastricht II treaty reforming the EU which is due to be signed in Amsterdam next week.
And, in remarks to reporters on Thursday, Lafontaine also supported Paris' demand to create a "European economic government" as a counterweight to Europe's planned independent central bank.
"Politicians can make mistakes -- but so can institutions which are apparently independent," he said in Saarbruecken, capital of the Saar state on the French border where he is also premier.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Wednesday conceded that Bonn would be ready to sign an employment chapter in Maastricht II. But Kinkel refused any further financial commitments on top of existing regional EU aid. Germany is the largest net contributor to the Brussels budget.

Lafontaine, repeating his earlier position, said he opposed delaying the start of EMU if countries could not meet exactly the budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product set by the Maastricht treaty this year.
"It doesn't depend on three-point-zero," he said in Saarbruecken.
That view clashes with the position held by Lafontaine's main rival for the SPD leadership, Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, who has suggested delaying the project.
"I share his concerns about stability. And in that, the leading Social Democrats in Europe are united. But also in that we should hold to the timetable," Lafontaine told Die Woche.
Elections in Germany are expected in September next year.
Lafontaine said he hoped Italy and Spain would join EMU from the start -- something many in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government want to hinder due to the countries' past fiscal profligacy.
"It would be desirable," he told Die Woche.

"The decisive criteria for monetary stability are not budget deficits, but exchange and interest rates and prices. Here in Europe a degree of stability has been achieved which many observers did not think possible years ago."
